strengths: Significance: A single routing policy covering 11 training tasks and 96 unseen variants is a useful engineering contribution. The evaluation spans asymmetric costs, pickup–delivery relations, multiple depots, and several constraint combinations.

Soundness: Several results demonstrate meaningful gains. On MDCVRP, URS achieves a 9.65% gap versus 17.37% for ReLD-MTL (Table 3). On large CVRPLIB instances, its average gap is 8.678%, compared with 12.836% for LEHD (Table 12).

Originality: Combining unified node features, directional and relational attention biases, and conditional decoder generation offers a plausible approach to broadening a shared solver. The component ablations support the usefulness of node-type indicators and the combined bias channels on seen tasks.

Presentation and reproducibility: The architecture is reasonably well organized, with extensive tables, feature definitions, data-generation descriptions, and training hyperparameters. Appendix L documents resource licenses; no material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—unsupported feasibility claim: Section 4 and Appendix G do not establish that LLM-generated masks guarantee feasible solutions. The only concrete example is a TSP visited-node mask. There are no reported generation success rates, held-out feasibility rates, failure cases, or checks for overly restrictive masks. Passing finitely many solution checks does not guarantee correctness or prevent construction dead ends under coupled constraints. This is a central claimed contribution, not a peripheral omission.

Reproducibility of constraint automation is inadequate: The manuscript does not specify the LLM/version, generation settings, search budget, validation-set size and separation from evaluation data, or complete prompts and checkers for the complex variants. It is unclear which reported experiments actually used generated masks. Problem-specific checkers also retain domain-engineering requirements that the claimed automation does not account for.

Significance—solution quality is substantially less consistent than claimed: Table 11 reports gaps of 37.63% on AOCVRP, 47.80% on AMDOCVRPL, and 48.02% on AMDOCVRP. Several asymmetric multi-depot evaluations also take longer than the listed reference solver. These difficult cases are absent from the main Table 3 selection. The claim of consistently high-quality, efficient solutions across more than 100 variants needs qualification and a representative aggregate analysis.

Originality and scope: UDR still uses a fixed, manually defined feature vocabulary, structural node roles, and a 13-dimensional feature-presence vector. The experiments demonstrate transfer within combinations of ten predefined constraint families, rather than an open-ended representation of new attributes or objectives. Zero-shot reuse of neural weights is valuable, but new masks, state handling, and checkers remain necessary. The distinction from prior constraint-combination approaches is overstated.

Causal evidence for zero-shot generalization is incomplete: All component ablations evaluate the 11 seen tasks. There is no direct ablation of conditional parameter generation against shared fixed parameters, and no unseen-task ablation establishing which components produce the claimed generalization gains. Appendix K.4 retains the hypernetwork in every decoder comparison. Training-seed variability and uncertainty estimates are also absent.

Evaluation and limitations need strengthening: RouteFinder and CaDA are excluded because their training setups differ, without controlled retraining or a sufficiently detailed matched-task comparison. Reference solutions are heuristic, so the reported gaps are not certified optimality gaps. The limitations discussion addresses only training efficiency, overlooking the fixed representation scope, poor performance on several unseen variants, and unverified mask reliability. Together, these issues prevent the otherwise promising system from supporting its strongest conclusions.

strengths: Significance: A single routing policy covering symmetric, asymmetric, pickup–delivery, and multi-depot problems is practically useful. Evaluation on 11 training variants and 96 unseen variants, with 1,000 instances per variant, provides substantial breadth.

Soundness: The reported results demonstrate meaningful gains on some unseen problems. For MDCVRP, URS achieves a 9.65% reference gap versus 17.37% for ReLD-MTL (Table 3). On large CVRPLIB instances, its average gap is 8.678%, compared with 12.836% for LEHD and 12.303% for RF-TE (Table 12).

Originality: Combining unified node features, incoming/outgoing distance biases, relational information, and feature-conditioned parameter generation is a useful architectural synthesis. The component ablations support benefits on trained tasks: removing node-type indicators increases average gap from 2.74% to 3.78%, and removing the relation channel increases it to 4.07%.

Presentation and reproducibility: The framework is reasonably well organized, with architecture diagrams, mathematical descriptions, data-generation conventions, and detailed training hyperparameters. Appendix L documents resource licenses; the manuscript raises no evident material research-ethics concern.
weaknesses: Soundness—unsupported feasibility guarantee: Section 4 and the conclusion claim that LLM-generated masks guarantee feasibility, but Appendix G provides only a basic TSP example. The paper reports no mask-generation success rates, held-out feasibility rates, failure cases, or comparison with verified masks across the complex variants. Passing finite solution checks cannot establish correctness for unseen instances; locally permissible actions can also lead to dead ends unless completion feasibility is addressed. This is a central unsupported claim.

Reproducibility of the LLM component is inadequate: The LLM identity/version, generation settings, search budget, validation-set size and separation from evaluation data, complex-variant prompts, generated masks, and checker implementations are not specified. Consequently, readers cannot establish how much of the reported evaluation actually uses automatically generated masks or reproduce the claimed reduction in manual constraint engineering. Problem-specific checkers and state bookkeeping still require domain knowledge.

Originality and scope: The evidence supports transfer within a fixed feature vocabulary, rather than the claimed open-ended constraint coverage. UDR uses predefined attributes and node roles, and its 13-dimensional conditioning vector records their presence; training explicitly exposes every feature. New attributes outside this vocabulary cannot simply be incorporated by zero-filling. Some variants have identical feature-presence vectors, leaving their distinction to external masks. This does not invalidate the useful transfer results, but it substantially narrows the claimed departure from predefined constraint representations.

Causal evidence for zero-shot generalization is missing: All component ablations in Section 6 and Appendix K concern the 11 seen tasks. There is no direct ablation of adaptive parameter generation against shared fixed parameters, or of feature-presence conditioning against problem tags, on unseen tasks. Decoder comparisons retain hypernetwork conditioning. Thus the experiments do not establish that the proposed representation and parameter generator cause the headline generalization benefits.

Significance is overstated by the claim of consistently high-quality solutions. Table 11 reports gaps of 37.63% on AOCVRP, 47.80% on AMDOCVRPL, and 48.02% on AMDOCVRP; several asymmetric multi-depot runs also take longer than the listed reference solver. Table 10 shows URS trailing ReLD-MTL on multiple familiar combinations, including OCVRPBTW (13.77% versus 9.29%). These results warrant a more qualified account of where the method is useful.

Evaluation controls are incomplete: RouteFinder and CaDA are excluded from the main comparison because their training setups differ, but the paper does not provide controlled retraining or sufficiently detailed adaptation protocols for the included baselines on new constraints. The 52 newly introduced variants lack competing neural baselines. Reported gaps are relative to heuristic references, not certified optima, and the repeated 6.6-minute reference timings need reconciliation with the stated single-core, 20-second-per-instance protocol. No training-seed variability or uncertainty estimates are provided.

Presentation and limitations: The limitations discussion addresses training efficiency but omits the fixed representation scope, unverified mask reliability, substantial worst-case gaps, and residual manual checker requirements. These omissions matter because they qualify the central claims. Overall, the architectural merits and broad experiments do not compensate for the unresolved feasibility, attribution, and reproducibility issues.

strengths: Significance: A single routing policy evaluated on 11 training variants and 96 unseen variants is a useful contribution toward reducing per-problem retraining. The coverage includes asymmetric costs, pickup–delivery relations, and multiple depots.

Soundness: Several results demonstrate substantial improvements over compared neural baselines. For MDCVRP, URS achieves a 9.65% gap versus ReLD-MTL’s 17.37% (Table 3). On large CVRPLIB instances, its average gap is 8.678%, compared with 12.303% for RF-TE and 12.836% for LEHD (Table 12).

Originality: Combining feature-presence conditioning, generated decoder parameters, and outgoing, incoming, and relational biases provides a plausible integration for broader routing generalization. Table 15 supports the complementary utility of these biases, reducing the average seen-task gap from 6.33% with outgoing distances alone to 2.74% with all three.

Presentation and reproducibility: The manuscript has an understandable architectural description and extensive per-variant results. Appendices document feature encodings, data-generation conventions, and training hyperparameters. Resource licenses and writing-assistance usage are disclosed; no material research-ethics concern is evident.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central claim that LLM-generated masks guarantee feasibility is unsupported. Section 4 and Appendix G describe a generate-and-validate procedure but provide only a basic TSP example, without identifying the LLM, generation budget, validation sample sizes, per-variant success rates, or held-out feasibility results. Passing finitely many solution checks does not establish that a mask always permits feasible completion or handles construction dead ends. The dependence on problem-specific checkers also leaves substantial domain engineering unexplained.

Originality and scope: The claimed move beyond predefined constraint combinations is overstated. UDR fixes six attributes and five node-role indicators, and training explicitly exposes every feature at least once. Evaluation largely recombines these predefined ingredients while supplying new constraint masks. This supports compositional transfer within the representation, but does not demonstrate open-ended incorporation of genuinely new attributes or constraints. Zero-filling cannot introduce an attribute for which no input slot exists.

Soundness: The ablations do not isolate the mechanisms claimed to enable zero-shot generalization. Tables 4 and 13–16 evaluate only seen tasks, and there is no ablation removing the parameter generator or comparing feature-presence conditioning against problem tags under matched training. Consequently, the evidence does not establish that UDR and adaptive parameter generation cause the reported unseen-task gains.

Significance and claim calibration: Solution quality is markedly uneven. Table 11 reports gaps of 37.63% on AOCVRP and 48.02% on AMDOCVRP; the latter also takes 7.8 minutes versus 6.6 minutes for the reference solver. Table 10 shows URS trailing ReLD-MTL on several standard combinations, including OCVRPBTW (13.77% versus 9.29%). These results qualify the repeated claim of consistently high-quality, efficient solutions across the full suite.

Evaluation and reproducibility: RouteFinder and CaDA are excluded from the main comparisons because of training differences, but matched-training comparisons with these relevant methods are not supplied. How other baselines are extended to unseen multi-depot constraints is insufficiently documented. The 52 newly introduced variants have no neural comparison, and gaps are relative to time-limited heuristics rather than certified optima. Missing independent-run variability and incomplete mask-generation artifacts further limit confidence and reproducibility.

Presentation and limitations: The limitations discussion addresses training efficiency but omits the consequential restrictions on representational coverage, mask reliability, and poor performance on some unseen families. Architectural and experimental promise does not compensate for these unresolved central evidential gaps; acceptance requires stronger validation and narrower claims.

strengths: Significance: A single trained policy covering symmetric, asymmetric, prize-collecting, and pickup-delivery routing is a useful contribution. Evaluation on 110 variants, including 99 held-out variants, substantially broadens the empirical scope of multi-task neural routing.

Soundness: The component ablations provide evidence that the design choices help. Table 7 reports reductions in unseen-task average gap from 10.41% without MBM to 7.05% with the full model; removing either parameter-generation component also worsens performance. Appendix J.2 additionally compares retrained RouteFinder and CaDA under aligned training settings.

Significance: The scale-generalization results are promising. Table 5 shows approximately stable 8–9% gaps on CVRPTW and OCVRPTW from 1,000 to 5,000 nodes, while several neural baselines deteriorate substantially. Table 6 reports a 13.29% average gap on four large CVRPLib instances, outperforming the listed neural competitors.

Originality: Although the underlying attention mechanism and hypernetwork techniques build on prior work, combining incoming/outgoing distance biases, relational information, and feature-conditioned decoding into one transferable routing policy is a meaningful architectural contribution.

Presentation and reproducibility: The paper is generally well organized and supplies extensive architectural details, training hyperparameters, data-generation references, and per-problem results. Resource licenses are documented, and no material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness and reproducibility: The feasibility mechanism is central but insufficiently specified. Sections 3.1 and E.3 delegate constraints to problem-specific masks without providing complete masking/state-update algorithms or reporting independently checked feasibility rates. Moreover, Equation (10) masks only previously visited nodes, not all constraint-infeasible nodes. Masking the attention aggregation in Equation (9) does not itself prevent an infeasible node from receiving positive final selection probability. The equation also needs to distinguish revisitable depots from customers. This may be a specification error, but it must be resolved before the claimed feasible solution generation across 110 variants can be assessed reliably.

Originality and claim scope: UDR remains a manually designed, fixed feature schema with explicit node roles, relation matrices, and a 13-dimensional presence vector. All feature types are exposed during training, and new constraints require externally implemented feasibility logic. Thus the results support transfer within an engineered interface, rather than the claimed open-ended replacement of predefined constraint sets or elimination of additional domain knowledge. Adding genuinely new attributes cannot generally be accomplished by zero-filling the fixed projection matrices.

Significance and evidential support: 'Consistently high-quality' zero-shot solutions overstates the results. Table 16 reports gaps of 43.79% on APCTSP and 39.31% on AMDOCVRPBP, while ASPCTSP has no reference comparison. Table 15 also shows that URS trails ReLD-MTL on multiple conventional unseen variants, including CVRPBTW and OCVRPBLTW. Breadth is valuable, but coverage, competitive quality, and uniformly strong generalization should be distinguished.

Experimental attribution: The principal cross-problem ablations cover only 11 unseen conventional CVRP variants, omitting the asymmetric, multi-depot, and pickup-delivery combinations that motivate the broader contribution. Scale-dependent attention is inherited from Zhou et al. (2026), yet the large-scale evaluation does not isolate its contribution from MBM and UDR. Targeted ablations on these harder families and at larger scales are needed to substantiate the proposed explanation for the gains.

Comparison and reproducibility: The adaptations that enable existing neural baselines to handle unseen multi-depot and precedence settings are not adequately documented. Appendix J.2 improves comparability, but its shared hyperparameters and 150-epoch stopping point following RouteFinder instability do not establish each baseline's best attainable performance. The manuscript also provides no URS implementation/checkpoint location or repeated-training uncertainty estimates, making smaller improvements difficult to assess.

Presentation and limitations: Several technical details require clarification. Equation (13) contains only consecutive affine transformations despite being described as an MLP hypernetwork; any nonlinearities should be specified. The reported gaps are generally relative to heuristic references, not certified optima. The limitations discussion appropriately acknowledges training imbalance, but should also address dependence on handcrafted masks, the fixed representation, and the substantial failures on some unseen variants. Together with the feasibility specification gap, these issues warrant revision before acceptance.

strengths: Significance: A single trained solver covering symmetric, asymmetric, pickup–delivery, and multi-depot routing is a useful contribution. Evaluation on 110 variants, including 99 held-out variants, substantially broadens the empirical scope of multi-task neural routing.

Soundness: The component ablations provide meaningful evidence. In Table 7, the full model reduces the average unseen-problem gap from 10.41% without MBM to 7.05%; removing either parameter-generation component also worsens performance. Appendix J.2 includes valuable comparisons with retrained RouteFinder and CaDA under matched training settings.

Scalability: Table 5 demonstrates relatively stable gaps on three routing families from 1,000 to 5,000 nodes. On Set-AGS, URS achieves a 13.29% average gap and processes instances up to 7,000 nodes, outperforming the reported neural comparators.

Presentation and originality: The architecture is generally well organized and combines unified node features, directional and relational biases, and conditional parameter generation coherently. The contribution is primarily this integration and its demonstrated breadth. Appendices document substantial architectural, training, and data-generation detail, and resource licenses are listed. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: The central generalization claim exceeds the evidence. Section 3.1 describes an open-ended problem space and substantially reduced domain expertise, but UDR contains a fixed set of handcrafted attributes and node roles, while problem-specific constraints are implemented through external masks. Appendix D explicitly constructs the test suite from combinations of ten predefined constraint categories. This supports broad compositional transfer with supplied constraint logic, rather than general handling of new constraint semantics. Zero-filling also cannot introduce an arbitrary new attribute into the fixed-dimensional projection in Equation (1).

Feasibility enforcement is insufficiently specified for a central part of the method. Equation (10) excludes visited nodes but does not apply the full feasibility mask to the final selection logits; masking the preceding attention in Equation (9) does not itself guarantee feasible selections. The equation also needs an exception for repeated depot visits. The manuscript should specify the actual final mask, state transitions, and handling of dead ends for compound constraints, and report independent feasibility checks. This may be a notation omission, but the current description does not establish the claimed guarantee.

The claim of consistently high-quality solutions is not supported across the full suite. Table 16 reports gaps of 43.79% on APCTSP, 47.86% on AMDOCVRPL, and 48.02% on AMDCVRPBP; ASPCTSP has no reference result. Several asymmetric multi-depot cases also take longer than the reported classical reference. These results demonstrate coverage, but considerably weaker optimization quality than the abstract and conclusion imply. The limitations discussion acknowledges training imbalance but should also address these observed performance boundaries.

Experimental attribution remains incomplete. The broadest asymmetric and pickup–delivery combinations lack neural comparators, while the main generalization ablations cover only 11 unseen conventional CVRP variants. Removing input attributes establishes their usefulness but does not isolate the benefit of UDR over a comparably expressive feature representation with the same masks and training tasks. Additional controlled comparisons are needed to distinguish architectural improvements from broader training coverage and supplied feasibility logic.

Reproducibility and uncertainty need improvement. No URS implementation or trained-checkpoint link is provided, and training-seed variability and confidence intervals are not reported. Classical heuristic references are described as oracles and their relative differences as optimality gaps without optimality certification. Runtime reporting also needs clarification: Section 4.1 specifies single-core classical runs with 20-second limits, whereas several 1,000-instance tables report 6.6-minute totals. Together with the unspecified masking implementation, these gaps prevent a sufficiently reliable assessment despite the substantial experimental work.

strengths: Significance: Training one model on 11 variants and evaluating it on 99 unseen variants is a substantial empirical undertaking. Extending coverage to asymmetric costs and pickup–delivery relations is useful beyond conventional CVRP constraint combinations.

Soundness: Component ablations support the architecture. Table 7 shows that the full model reduces the average gap on 11 unseen variants from 10.41% without MBM to 7.05%; removing either parameter-generation component also degrades performance.

Scalability is a convincing strength within the tested settings. Table 5 shows substantially better large-instance performance than the compared multitask neural solvers, and Table 6 reports a 13.29% average gap on four 3,000–7,000-node benchmarks, versus 22.22% for LEHD.

Originality: The integration of a shared feature representation, directional and relational attention biases, and conditional decoder generation provides a useful architectural contribution, even though its individual ingredients build on established methods.

Presentation and reproducibility: The paper is generally readable, with extensive appendices specifying feature encodings, instance generation, hyperparameters, training costs, and additional comparisons. Appendix J.2 makes a worthwhile effort to address compatibility differences with RouteFinder and CaDA.

Research ethics: No material ethical concerns are apparent for the reported experiments. The resource-license inventory is helpful, and the acknowledged training-efficiency limitations are appropriate.
weaknesses: The central generalization claim exceeds the demonstrated scope. UDR uses a fixed, manually designed attribute vocabulary, while problem-specific constraints are delegated to externally implemented masks. This supports transfer across supported constraint combinations, but does not establish an open-ended solver or substantially eliminate domain expertise. The paper should explicitly distinguish learned transfer from capability supplied by the constraint environment.

Feasibility is insufficiently specified for a contribution centered on broad constraint coverage. Equation (10) masks only previously visited nodes; masking the attention in Equation (9) alone does not prevent the final softmax from selecting a constraint-violating node. Equation (10) also does not explain repeated depot visits. These may be notation omissions, but complete masking/state-update rules, dead-end handling, and independent feasibility checks are needed to substantiate the claimed guarantees across 110 variants.

The claim of consistently high-quality unseen solutions is not supported uniformly. Table 16 reports gaps of 37.63% on AOCVRP, 47.80% on AMDOCVRPL, and 48.02% on AMDOCVRP. Table 15 also shows numerous unseen variants where ReLD-MTL performs better. Moreover, the reported 'optimality gaps' generally use heuristic references, not certified optima. The results establish breadth more convincingly than uniformly strong solution quality.

The most distinctive transfer claims lack targeted attribution. The unseen-task component ablations cover 11 conventional CVRP variants, rather than the asymmetric and pickup–delivery combinations emphasized as new capabilities. Removing input attributes also changes available information, so those ablations do not isolate the advantage of UDR over another shared representation. Matched experiments on these distinctive unseen families would strengthen the contribution substantially.

Reproducibility and comparison uncertainty remain material. The manuscript does not provide a URS implementation/checkpoint link, repeated-training variability, or confidence intervals. Adaptations enabling baseline solvers to handle additional constraints are not sufficiently documented. Appendix J.2's matched retraining helps, but truncating all methods at 150 epochs following RouteFinder instability does not establish their converged relative performance. Together with the feasibility ambiguity, these gaps require revision before the broad generalization results can be relied upon confidently.
